mappings.note: Identify acid, base and water with red litmus alone. Distinguishing acids from bases with an indicator is LO-3; working out a procedure with only one indicator is inquiry design, cited at C 8.2 (its LO-1 is specifically pH testing of household substances, which this is not).
Sour foods attack brass and copper. The reaction of an acid with a metal, LO-3.
Hydrogen from acid plus metal, with an example and the pop test. LO-3 for the reaction and its test; the illustrating equation is C 1.3-LO-3.
Balanced equation for a carbonate plus dilute HCl giving CaCl2 and CO2. The demand is the equation, so C 1.3-LO-3 rather than the descriptive LO-3 of C 1.2.
Why HCl is acidic but ethanol and glucose are not -- only the former releases H+ in water. Acidic nature tied to hydrogen-ion concentration, LO-4.
Acids conduct because they furnish ions in water. Same H+ basis of acidity as LO-4; no indicator or reaction is involved, so not LO-3.
Dry HCl gas leaves dry litmus unchanged -- without water there are no H+ ions and so no acidic character. LO-4.

Why acid is added to water, never the reverse. This is the heat of dilution of a concentrated acid -- a property of the substance with no learning outcome in this frame, so the C 1.2 competency is cited.
What dilution does to hydronium-ion concentration. Directly the H+ basis of LO-4.
What more base does to hydroxide-ion concentration. The basic side of LO-4.
pH 6 versus pH 8: which holds more H+ and which is acidic. LO-4 verbatim.
Effect of H+ concentration on acidic strength. LO-4.
Whether basic solutions contain H+ and why they are still basic. The relative H+/OH- balance behind the pH scale, LO-4.
When a farmer limes a field -- when the soil is too acidic. Soil pH is one of the everyday-pH cases LO-4 covers; the demand is the pH judgement, not an equation.
Dry slaked lime plus chlorine gives bleaching powder, with the equation. Preparation of bleaching powder, named in LO-5.
Washing soda softens hard water. A use of washing soda, LO-5.
Equation for plaster of Paris setting with water. Properties of plaster of Paris, named in LO-5; the equation is incidental to the substance.
Red litmus turning blue implies a pH well above 7. The verdict asked for is a pH value, so LO-4 rather than the indicator outcome LO-3.
Egg shells fizzing to give a gas that turns lime water milky identifies HCl. Acid on a carbonate, LO-3.
Doubling the NaOH doubles the HCl needed. Proportional reasoning about acid neutralising base -- LO-3's 'reactions with each other'. Not C 1.3-LO-3, since no equation is written.
Antacid for indigestion. One of the everyday-pH applications of LO-4 (excess stomach acid).

Devise an activity proving alcohol and glucose are not acids. Content is the H+ criterion for acidity (LO-4); designing the conductivity activity is C 8.2, since C 8.2-LO-1 is restricted to pH testing of household substances.
Distilled water does not conduct, rain water does, because rain water carries dissolved acidic gases and so ions. LO-4's H+ basis.
No water, no acidic behaviour -- acids need water to ionise. LO-4.
Sorts five pH readings into neutral, weakly/strongly acidic and alkaline and orders them by H+. LO-4 in full.
Magnesium fizzes harder in HCl than in acetic acid. The reaction with a metal is LO-3; the reason -- a strong acid supplies more H+ -- is LO-4.
How milk's pH moves as it sours. A pH judgement, LO-4.
Baking soda raising milk's pH and delaying curdling. The pH reasoning is LO-4; baking soda and its uses are LO-5.
Why plaster of Paris needs a dry container -- it sets with moisture. A property of plaster of Paris, LO-5.
Defines neutralisation with examples. 'Acids and bases reacting with each other' is LO-3; the question asks what it is, not for a balanced equation.
Two uses each of washing soda and baking soda. LO-5 verbatim. (The stem has swallowed the answer text of a neighbouring neutralisation item -- see defect list.)
Water poured into syrupy conc. sulphuric acid, cracking the tube and causing burns. Heat of dilution and corrosiveness -- properties with no outcome in this frame, so the competency, as with 84916.
The missing ingredient that makes a cake fluffy is baking powder, whose hydrogencarbonate gives CO2. A use of baking soda, LO-5.
A building material giving CO2 with dilute HCl is calcium carbonate -- the acid-carbonate reaction of LO-3 -- and the question also demands the chemical equations, C 1.3-LO-3.

Sodium hydroxide from the chlor-alkali process, whose products feed the bleaching-powder and washing-soda chemistry of LO-5; the neutralisation of X with dilute HCl must be written as an equation, C 1.3-LO-3. The closing dilution-safety part has no outcome and is left uncited.
Four indicator observations (litmus, methyl orange, phenolphthalein) on known solutions. Distinguishing acids from bases with indicators, LO-3.
Burns from boiling concentrated sulphuric acid. The corrosive nature of a concentrated acid, a substance property with no outcome here; competency cited.
Excess stomach acid treated with an antacid -- everyday pH, LO-4 -- plus the explicit request for the chemical equation of the neutralisation, C 1.3-LO-3.
Wasp sting neutralised by a mildly basic toothpaste. One of LO-4's everyday-pH cases.
Mixing acid and base warms the mixture and makes a salt. Neutralisation described, LO-3.
Which addition reverses a blue-litmus change -- hydrochloric acid. Indicator reading plus neutralisation, LO-3.
Anhydrous calcium chloride drying HCl gas. A drying agent's behaviour is a substance property with no learning outcome in this frame; cited at the C 1.2 competency.
Which of blue vitriol, baking soda, washing soda and gypsum lacks water of crystallisation. Three of the four are LO-5 substances and the answer turns on their formulae, so LO-5.
Sodium carbonate is basic because it comes from a weak acid and a strong base. The pH of a salt solution, LO-4.
Nature of calcium phosphate in enamel. Part of LO-4's tooth-decay pH case.
Reads a pH-paper colour on a soil extract and picks what would raise it. Relating colour to pH and to acidic/basic nature, LO-4.
Increasing order of acidic strength across water, acetic acid and HCl. Strength as H+ concentration, LO-4. (Options are corrupted -- see defect list.)

First aid for an acid spill: water then a paste of sodium hydrogencarbonate. It is a neutralisation (LO-3) and the specific agent is baking soda (LO-5); the distractors punish reaching for a strong alkali.
Properties of the gas from sodium hydrogencarbonate and acetic acid. Identifying CO2 from an acid-carbonate reaction, LO-3.
Common salt as the feedstock for washing soda and baking soda. Preparation of LO-5's substances.
Tartaric acid is baking powder's second constituent. Composition and use of baking soda, LO-5.
Toothpaste is basic, to counter mouth acid. LO-4's tooth-decay case.
Which pH statements are correct. The pH scale itself, LO-4.
pH of gastric juice is below 7. Everyday pH, LO-4.
Adding a little acid to water causes ionisation and dilution, not neutralisation. Tests what acidity in water means, LO-4.
Which indicator a visually impaired student could use (an olfactory one). Indicators, LO-3.
Which substance gives no CO2 with dilute acid -- lime, not being a carbonate. The acid-carbonate reaction of LO-3.
Which of four everyday substances is acidic. Relating a substance to acidic or basic nature, LO-4.
Why the bulb glows with HCl -- a strong acid furnishes ions. Conduction as evidence of H+ in solution, LO-4.
